summary:
Amazonas stands under Brazil's national framework. Same-sex marriage has been legal nationwide since the National Council of Justice resolution of 14 May 2013, carried 14-1, joint adoption has been available since 2010 with full rights from 2015, and legal gender change requires no surgery, hormones or diagnosis following the Supreme Federal Tribunal ruling of 1 March 2018.

On 13 June 2019 the Supreme Federal Court, in the ADO 26 and MI 4733 proceedings, held discrimination and violence on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity a crime equivalent to racism under Law 7.716/1989, punishable by imprisonment and fines. An expatriate legal guide updated in April 2026 puts the term at one to five years and confirms that same-sex marriage, spousal-visa equality and gender-marker rules operate nationwide, so a visitor's status and documents are handled on the same footing as anyone else's at entry and in family matters.

No third-gender marker is available nationally, but civil registries have recorded non-binary or unspecified entries since 2020, and a Superior Court of Justice ruling of 6 May 2025 permits rectification of a registry entry to a neutral gender as precedent.

Arrest and imprisonment carry a defined regime. National Council of Justice Resolution 348 of 13 October 2020, amended by Resolution 366 of 20 January 2021, governs where LGBTI people who are arrested or imprisoned are housed. A person is recognised as LGBTI for these purposes by self-declaration before a judge, including at a custody hearing; the placement is fixed by a reasoned decision taken after the person has been consulted about their preference, and the declared preference is recorded and may be changed later. LGBTI-specific living spaces may not be used as disciplinary isolation, and compulsory transfer as punishment is prohibited.

The protective text does not describe what people routinely encounter. OutRight International's country report states that Brazil retains one of the world's highest rates of violence against sexual and gender minorities, particularly trans people, notwithstanding the constitutional and criminal provisions.

The expatriate guide records uneven enforcement as a feature of the current regime: major cities are broadly welcoming with established legal infrastructure, while smaller cities and rural areas may present more social friction despite identical legal rights. The sources assembled for this record contain no Amazonas-specific evidence identifying which condition holds in which part of the state.
tangentialFactors:
The advances described above face repeal pressure in a conservative Congress, according to OutRight International's country report, so the statutory framework in force is contested rather than settled.

Violence is documented at specific sites. A May 2024 investigation recorded drink-spiking robberies in which LGBTQIA+ people are targeted in the nightlife of a major city preparing for a Pride event that draws thousands of tourists.

Election periods have carried a distinct threat pattern. In the October 2024 municipal elections close to 1,000 transgender candidates stood across every state of the country and received death threats and intimidation, while the number of trans officeholders tripled against the previous cycle; more than 3,000 openly LGBTQ candidates ran in the same elections. The first transgender federal legislators, Salabert and Hilton, were elected in 2022.

Placement practice in one state's prison system shows how far administration can depart from the national rule. A peer-reviewed census carried out between April and June 2021 interviewed 138 self-declared travesti and trans-woman inmates inside eleven units treated as masculine in a metropolitan prison region, finding travestis and trans women housed in masculine-designated units or in so-called neutral and security units, and treating placement in male units as a double punishment compounded by recurring violations of basic rights. The same study notes a 2015 state law granting parity of treatment with cisgender women in women's units, covering hair length, feminine clothing, accessories and cosmetics, alongside national norms from 2014 and 2020 permitting people to be housed where they choose.

Protection machinery has widened in the courts: an analysis of case law from 2022 records lower courts pressing the Superior Court of Justice toward unanimously extending the remedies of the Maria da Penha Law and the Feminicide Law to trans women.

outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the live inventory addresses Amazonas specifically. State-level policing, court practice, hate-crime prosecutions and prison administration in Amazonas are not sourced, and the uneven-enforcement finding drawn from the expatriate guide is national in scope rather than a measurement of any part of the state.

The record contains no Amazonas-specific figure for violence against trans people, and the national violence rates cited come from a country-level report that does not disaggregate by state.

Whether Amazonas civil registries have in practice issued non-binary or neutral-gender entries since 2020, and whether the 6 May 2025 precedent has been applied here, remains unresolved on the available sources.

Application of National Council of Justice Resolutions 348 and 366 inside Amazonas detention facilities is not documented in the inventory; the Rio de Janeiro prison census is evidence from a different state and is used here only to show that practice can diverge from the national rule.
